name: Thimble Loop Rigging Sling 1/2 x 35 in with 28mm Ring
title: Thimble Loop Rigging Sling 1/2 x 35 in, 28mm Ring
h1: Thimble Loop Rigging Sling, 1/2 x 35 in with 28mm Ring
meta: A 1/2 x 35 in thimble loop rigging sling with a 28mm ring for choking a spar and running a lowering line. How it rigs, sizing, and what it costs.
tagline: A 1/2 rope sling with a thimble eye and 28mm ring for natural-crotch and spar rigging.
summary: This thimble loop rigging sling pairs 1/2 rope, a 35 in length, and a 28mm ring so you can choke a stem and set up a quick rigging point. The 1/2 in version is the lighter, easier-to-handle choice for pruning-size wood and small tops.
highlights: 1/2 rope body, 35 in long
Thimble-protected loop at one end
28mm ring for choking and redirecting
Quick to set and retrieve from the ground
Works as a rigging point or a choker on the piece

body.h: How a ring sling works on the job
p: A ring sling is the simplest way to build a rigging point where there is no good crotch. Wrap the stem, pass the thimble loop through the ring, and cinch it down; the ring then becomes the anchor for a block or a lowering line. Because it chokes, it holds its position on a vertical spar better than a basket hitch.

The thimble keeps the loop open and protects the rope where it bears on hardware, so you can clip a carabiner or shackle into it without crushing the eye. The 1/2 in version is the lighter, easier-to-handle choice for pruning-size wood and small tops. Keep the 35 in length in mind: it suits small to medium stems and will not wrap a large trunk.
Match the sling to the wood you are actually taking down and to the rest of the system, including the rope and block. Browse other heavy-duty rigging slings if you need longer or stronger options.

Check the rope for cut strands, glazing, and stiff spots, and look at the ring and thimble for grooves, cracks, or deformation before each job. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Can I use a ring sling as a choker on the piece?
faq.a: Yes. Many crews choke the piece with a ring sling and tie or clip the lowering line to it. Make sure the ring and rope are rated for the dynamic load of the piece being cut.

faq.q: What does the 28mm refer to?
faq.a: It describes the ring size listed for this sling. Confirm the ring's rated strength with the seller before using it in a rigging system.

name: 5/8 in Bull Rope Thimble Sling with Large Ring
title: 5/8 in Bull Rope Sling with Thimble and Large Ring
h1: 5/8 in Bull Rope Sling with Thimble and Large Ring
meta: A 5/8 in bull rope sling with a thimble eye and large ring for heavy rigging points and chokers. Learn where it fits, what to check, and typical price.
tagline: Heavy 5/8 in bull rope sling with a thimble and big ring for real wood.
summary: This bull rope sling is built from 5/8 in rigging rope with a thimble eye and a large ring, sized for removals where you are lowering heavy wood. The bigger ring passes a thick rope tail easily and gives a solid point for a block or lowering line.
highlights: 5/8 in bull rope body
Thimble-protected eye
Large ring for choking and clipping
Suited to heavy removals and big spars
Can serve as a rigging point or a choker

body.h: Where a 5/8 in sling earns its keep
p: Once the wood gets heavy, a light sling becomes the weak link. A 5/8 in bull rope sling gives you more strength and more abrasion resistance around rough bark, and the large ring lets the eye pass through cleanly so the choke sets tight on a vertical spar.

Use it to build a rigging point for a block high on the stem, or choke the piece and tie the lowering line to the ring. The thimble keeps the eye round under load, so a shackle or steel carabiner sits properly and the rope is not pinched. On a long removal, that durability means one sling can handle pick after pick without being swapped out.

Size every part of the system to the heaviest piece you plan to drop, including the block, lowering device, and rope. Compare lengths and strengths among other heavy-duty slings before you commit to one.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands looking for cut or melted strands, hardened sections, and wear at the thimble. Look over the ring for nicks and deformation. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is a 5/8 in sling overkill for pruning?
faq.a: Usually. For small limbs a 1/2 in sling is lighter and easier to handle. The 5/8 in sling makes sense for removals and heavy rigging.

faq.q: Does it need a block?
faq.a: No. You can choke the piece or run a lowering line through a natural crotch, but a block on the sling reduces friction and wear on the tree.

name: Double-Headed Rigging Sling, 5/8 in x 15 ft
title: Double-Headed Rigging Sling 5/8 in x 15 ft
h1: Double-Headed Rigging Sling, 5/8 in x 15 ft
meta: A 5/8 in x 15 ft double-headed rigging sling with an eye at each end for wrapping big stems, hanging blocks, and choking wood. How it rigs and price.
tagline: A long 5/8 in sling with an eye at each end for big stems and heavy blocks.
summary: This double-headed rigging sling is 15 ft of 5/8 in rope with a spliced eye at both ends, long enough to wrap a large trunk several times or set a block on a wide stem. It is a go-to choice when a short ring sling will not reach around.
highlights: 5/8 in rope, 15 ft long
Spliced eye at each end
Long enough for large-diameter stems
Works for blocks, lowering devices, and chokers
Can be wrapped for extra friction

body.h: Rigging with a long two-eye sling
p: A double eye sling is the flexible option in a rigging kit. On a big trunk you can wrap it several times and girth the eyes together, which spreads the load and keeps the sling from sliding down the stem. Clip a block between the eyes, or set a lowering device on the base of the tree.

Fifteen feet gives you room to work around wide stems and odd unions where a short ring sling simply will not reach. The 5/8 in diameter suits removals and heavier wood rather than light pruning work. It is also handy as a temporary anchor for a lowering device at the base when the trunk is too wide for a short strap.

body.h: Setup, care, and when to retire it
p: Keep the eyes clean and free of twists when you clip them so the load sits evenly. If you need a shorter or ring-ended option for small stems, look through the other heavy-duty rigging slings.

Inspect the full length before each job for cuts, chainsaw nicks, melted spots, and pulled strands, paying close attention to the splices. Store it dry and out of the sun. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: How do I attach a block to a double eye sling?
faq.a: A common method is to wrap the stem, bring both eyes together, and clip them into the block's side plates or a rated shackle. Follow the block maker's instructions.

faq.q: Is 15 ft too long for small trees?
faq.a: It can be awkward on small stems. Extra wraps take up length, but a shorter sling is quicker for pruning-size work.

name: Tylaska TFB-20 Cerberus Rigging Block
title: Tylaska TFB-20 Cerberus Rigging Block
meta: The Tylaska TFB-20 Cerberus is a machined low-friction rigging block for arborist lowering systems. See how it rigs, what to check, and typical price today.
tagline: A machined Tylaska friction block for building clean, low-wear rigging points.
summary: The Tylaska TFB-20 Cerberus is a machined, low-friction rigging block for arborists who want a rigging point with no moving parts. It gives the lowering line a smooth bearing surface so the rope and the tree take less wear than in a natural crotch.
highlights: Machined low-friction rope bearing surface
No moving parts to wash out or seize
Lets rope run smoothly around a fixed surface
Compact enough to carry on a rigging kit
Pairs with a sling to build a rigging point

p: Tylaska is known for machined low-friction rings and fittings that started in sailing hardware and moved into tree work. The Cerberus TFB-20 applies that approach to a rigging block: hang it on a sling at the rigging point, run the lowering line through it, and let the groundie take the load at a lowering device.

A low-friction device sits between a pulley and a natural crotch. There are no bearings or sheaves, so it tolerates grit and sap well, and it is lighter than many blocks of similar size. The trade-off is more friction than a true pulley, which can help a groundie control a load but means more effort when hauling.

Many climbers also use low-friction devices for redirects and for small speedlines or retrievable setups, where a clean, snag-free surface matters more than raw efficiency. Because the device is a single machined piece, there are fewer things to check, but the rope-bearing surface still needs to stay smooth.

Pick a sling and connector rated for the loads you plan to put on the system, and confirm rope diameter compatibility with the manufacturer before you buy. Compare it with other rigging rings and hardware to see which style suits your work.

Check the rope-bearing surface for burrs, grooves, or rough spots that could damage rope, and retire the device if it is cracked or deformed. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is a low-friction ring the same as a pulley?
faq.a: No. It has no rotating sheave, so it adds some friction. That can be useful for controlling a lowering line, but a pulley is more efficient for hauling.

faq.q: What rope sizes does it take?
faq.a: Check Tylaska's published specifications for this model. Rope fit and rated strength vary by size, and the manufacturer's figures are the ones to follow.

name: DMM Anchor Rings, Matt Grey
title: DMM Anchor Ring, Matt Grey, for Tree Climbing
meta: DMM anchor rings in matt grey for friction savers, adjustable anchors, and spliced eyes. See how climbers use them, what to inspect, and the typical price.
tagline: Machined DMM rings for friction savers, anchors, and custom climbing setups.
summary: DMM anchor rings are machined rings that arborists use to build friction savers, adjustable tie-in anchors, and other custom climbing setups. The matt grey finish is a low-glare color option that is easy to tell apart from colored rings on a busy harness.
highlights: Machined one-piece ring from DMM
Matt grey finish
Smooth bore for rope and hitch cord
Used for friction savers and adjustable anchors
Easy to sort from colored rings

p: Rings show up all over a modern climbing kit. A pair of rings on a length of rope makes a ring-and-ring friction saver that you can set and retrieve from the ground. A single ring on a sling makes a canopy anchor, and rings are often used on adjustable SRS base anchors and lanyard setups.

Because a ring has no gate, it can take loading from several directions. The smooth bore lets rope and hitch cord run without catching, which matters when you retrieve a friction saver or advance a hitch around it. Having a few spare rings in the gear bag also makes it easy to build a quick redirect or replace a worn ring on a saver.

A neutral matt grey ring is a good way to keep track of which rings belong to which system. Some climbers use one color for friction savers and another for lanyards so they can grab the right piece at a glance.

Check the ring's rated strength and inner diameter before you build a system around it, and make sure it suits the rope and cord you will run through it. See the full range of climbing rings for other sizes and colors.

Retire rings with deep grooves from rope wear, sharp edges, cracks, or any deformation, and after a serious fall or impact. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use these rings for a ring-and-ring friction saver?
faq.a: Yes, that is a common use. Pair them with a rope or sling and build the saver following the maker's instructions and your training.

faq.q: Does the color affect strength?
faq.a: No. The finish is cosmetic. Strength comes from the ring's design and material, so check the marked rating.

name: All Gear Heavy Duty Rope Bag
title: All Gear Heavy Duty Rope Bag for Climbing Lines
h1: All Gear Heavy Duty Rope Bag
meta: The All Gear heavy duty rope bag keeps climbing and rigging lines clean, dry, and ready to deploy. Learn sizing, packing tips, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A tough rope bag for keeping climbing and rigging lines clean between jobs.
summary: The All Gear heavy duty rope bag gives a climbing or rigging line a clean place to live between jobs, away from chips, fuel, and sun. Flake the rope in, close it up, and it pays out cleanly at the next tree.
highlights: Heavy-duty construction for daily truck use
Keeps rope out of dirt, sap, and fuel
Rope flakes in and pays out without tangles
Carry handles for moving between trees
Helps rope last longer

p: Rope wears out from more than climbing. Grit works into the braid, chainsaw bar oil and fuel attack fibers, and UV fades and weakens the cover. A heavy duty rope bag keeps the line off the truck bed and out of the chip pile, so it lasts longer and is easier to inspect.
Flaking the rope straight into the bag, rather than coiling it, means it feeds back out without kinks. Leave the end with your termination on top so you can grab it and go at the next tree.

A sturdy bag also makes the truck safer and tidier. Rope that lives in a bag is not underfoot on the deck, is not wrapped around saw bars, and is not sitting in a puddle of bar oil. On a busy day, being able to toss one bag over a shoulder and walk to the next tree saves real time.
Choose a bag sized for your longest line with room to spare; a stuffed bag is slow to pack and hard to close. Compare capacities among other rope bags if you carry several ropes.

Empty the bag now and then to shake out sawdust, and let it dry if it gets wet before storing rope in it. Keep life-support rope separate from fuel cans and sharp tools, and inspect the rope itself before every climb.

faq.q: Should I flake or coil rope into the bag?
faq.a: Flake it. Feeding rope in loosely, hand over hand, lets it pay out cleanly later without twists.

faq.q: Can I store two ropes in one bag?
faq.a: It is possible but they tend to tangle. One rope per bag, or a bag with separate compartments, is faster on the job.

name: DMM Transit Rope Bag 30 L
title: DMM Transit Rope Bag 30 L for Arborists
meta: The DMM Transit rope bag in 30 L keeps climbing rope clean and organized between trees. See what fits, how it packs, and typical price in the US.
tagline: A 30 liter DMM rope bag for carrying and deploying climbing line.
summary: The DMM Transit rope bag in the 30 L size is a carry bag for climbing rope that keeps the line clean and ready to deploy. The 30 L size suits a single climbing line of moderate length and is compact enough to clip to a saddle or tuck behind the seat.
highlights: 30 liter capacity
Holds rope clean and off the ground
Easy to carry between trees
Rope pays out without tangles
Part of DMM's Transit bag range

body.h: Packing and using the Transit bag
p: Flake your rope in loosely, hand over hand, and leave the working end on top. At the next tree you open the bag and the line feeds out without the knots and twists you get from a coiled rope tossed in the truck.

The 30 L size suits a single climbing line of moderate length and is compact enough to clip to a saddle or tuck behind the seat. If you climb on one rope and rig with another, a second bag keeps them apart and makes it obvious which line is which.

A bag also protects rope from UV while it sits in the sun on the drop zone, and it keeps the line from being stepped on, driven over, or dragged through mud between trees. Those small savings add up to a longer service life for an expensive climbing line.
A bag that is too small is slow to pack and hard to close, so size up if you are unsure. See the other rope bags for more capacities.

Shake out sawdust regularly and let the bag dry before storing a rope in it. Keep climbing rope away from fuel, bar oil, and sharp tools, and inspect it before every climb; life-support rope must be retired if it shows cuts, glazing, or contamination.

faq.q: How much rope fits in the 30 L bag?
faq.a: It depends on rope diameter and length. Check DMM's capacity guidance, and allow some room so the rope is not crammed in.

faq.q: Is it only for climbing rope?
faq.a: No. It works for throw line, slings, or a short rigging line, but most climbers dedicate it to one climbing rope.

Easy to carry between trees
Rope pays out without tangles
Part of DMM's Transit bag range

body.h: Packing and using the Transit bag
p: Flake your rope in loosely, hand over hand, and leave the working end on top. At the next tree you open the bag and the line feeds out without the knots and twists you get from a coiled rope tossed in the truck.

The 45 L size gives room for a longer climbing line, or a rope plus a few small accessories, without cramming. If you climb on one rope and rig with another, a second bag keeps them apart and makes it obvious which line is which.

A bag also protects rope from UV while it sits in the sun on the drop zone, and it keeps the line from being stepped on, driven over, or dragged through mud between trees. Those small savings add up to a longer service life for an expensive climbing line.
A bag that is too small is slow to pack and hard to close, so size up if you are unsure. See the other rope bags for more capacities.

Shake out sawdust regularly and let the bag dry before storing a rope in it. Keep climbing rope away from fuel, bar oil, and sharp tools, and inspect it before every climb; life-support rope must be retired if it shows cuts, glazing, or contamination.

faq.q: How much rope fits in the 45 L bag?
faq.a: It depends on rope diameter and length. Check DMM's capacity guidance, and allow some room so the rope is not crammed in.

faq.q: Is it only for climbing rope?
faq.a: No. It works for throw line, slings, or a short rigging line, but most climbers dedicate it to one climbing rope.

name: Gap Arborist Supply Heavy Duty Bull Rope Bag
title: Heavy Duty Bull Rope Bag for Rigging Lines
meta: A heavy duty bull rope bag for storing and deploying thick rigging lines on removals. Learn what to look for, how to pack it, and the typical price.
tagline: A big, tough bag for thick rigging rope on removal jobs.
summary: A bull rope bag is a large, heavy duty bag for storing and deploying thick rigging lines on removals. It keeps a long, heavy rope out of the chips and lets the ground crew pay it out without a pile of tangles.
highlights: Sized for thick bull rope
Heavy-duty material for truck and ground use
Keeps rigging line clean and organized
Rope pays out smoothly to the climber
Carry handles for moving heavy rope
specs: Bull rope and thick rigging lines

body.h: Why rigging line needs its own bag
p: Bull rope takes a beating: it drags through dirt, runs over bark, and sits in the chip pile between picks. Grit inside the braid wears fibers from the inside, so keeping the line in a bag between jobs adds real life to an expensive rope.

A big bag also speeds the job. The groundie can feed rope up to the climber straight from the bag, and at the end of the day the line is flaked back in instead of wrapped around a forearm and thrown on the truck. A tidy drop zone is also a safer one, with less rope underfoot for the ground crew to trip on. Clearly separating rigging line from climbing line is another reason to give bull rope a bag of its own.
Flake the rope in from one end so the other end comes out first and clean. If you carry climbing lines too, keep them in separate rope bags so life-support rope never ends up mixed with rigging rope.
Dump the bag out periodically to clear sawdust and let it dry fully after wet days. Inspect the rope itself before every job for cuts, glazing, and stiff sections, and retire it when it is damaged.

faq.q: How much rope does a bull rope bag hold?
faq.a: It depends on the rope diameter and length. Check the bag's stated capacity against your longest rigging line and leave some room.

faq.q: Can I keep a climbing line in it?
faq.a: You can, but most crews keep climbing and rigging rope in separate bags so they are never confused.

name: High Wall Rope Thimble
title: High Wall Rope Thimble for Spliced Eyes
meta: A high wall rope thimble protects spliced eyes in rigging rope and slings from crushing and wear. Learn how it is used, sizing tips, and the typical price.
tagline: A deep-sided thimble that keeps rope seated in a spliced eye.
summary: A high wall rope thimble sits inside a spliced eye to keep the rope round and protected where it bears on hardware. The tall side walls hold the rope in the groove better than a standard thimble, which matters on synthetic rope under load.
highlights: Tall side walls keep rope seated
Protects spliced eyes from crushing and abrasion
Keeps the eye open for shackles and carabiners
Common on slings and rigging lines
Simple, durable hardware
specs: Synthetic rope slings and rigging lines

body.h: What a high wall thimble does
p: Every time a spliced eye is clipped to a shackle or block, the rope at the bearing point takes a tight bend and concentrated pressure. A thimble spreads that load around a curved groove, so the fibers are not crushed or cut, and the eye stays open for the next connection.

Standard thimbles were designed for wire rope, and soft synthetic rope can roll out of a shallow groove. The high wall design gives the rope deeper sides to sit in, which keeps it seated when the load shifts or the rope stretches. That is why you see them on ring slings, block slings, and the working ends of rigging lines.

Match the thimble to the rope diameter and to the pin or connector it will ride on; a thimble that is too small pinches the rope and one that is too big lets it shift. Find splicing tools and related hardware in rope care and splicing.

Splices must be made following the rope maker's splicing instructions. Inspect thimbles for cracks, sharp edges, and spreading, and replace them when worn. Rig only within the rated strength of every component in the system, inspect gear before each job, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging practice under ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Why use a high wall thimble instead of a standard one?
faq.a: The taller walls hold synthetic rope in the groove better, so the eye is less likely to roll out of the thimble under load.

faq.q: Can I add a thimble to an existing eye splice?
faq.a: Usually it has to be fitted while the splice is made. Re-splicing an eye should follow the rope maker's instructions.

name: Bandit Replacement Lanyard
title: Bandit Replacement Lanyard for Rope Positioning
meta: The Bandit replacement lanyard is a rope positioning lanyard for climbers who need to swap a worn line and keep their adjuster. Fit tips and typical price.

summary: The Bandit replacement lanyard is a rope positioning lanyard for climbers who want to replace a worn line while keeping their existing adjuster or hitch. It lets you refresh the part that wears without buying a whole new lanyard kit.
highlights: Replacement rope for a positioning lanyard
Spliced end for quick connection
Pairs with a mechanical adjuster or a hitch
Easy to spot on the stem
Keeps your existing hardware in service

p: Lanyard rope wears faster than almost anything else on a saddle. It is wrapped around rough bark, dragged across limbs, and constantly run through an adjuster. A replacement lanyard lets you retire the worn rope and keep your hardware, which is the cheapest way to stay on a lanyard you trust.

A good positioning lanyard should grip in an adjuster or hitch without slipping, run smoothly when you shorten it one-handed, and resist abrasion from bark. Remember that a lanyard is for work positioning, not fall arrest, and that around a saw you need a steel-core flipline or a second tie-in.

Many climbers prefer a lanyard length that wraps the largest stems they regularly work with a little to spare. Too short and you cannot get around a big trunk; too long and the tail gets in the way of the saw. Think about the trees you climb most when you choose.
Before buying, check that the rope diameter suits your adjuster or hitch cord. You can compare lengths and termination styles among other rope lanyards.

Inspect the lanyard before every climb for cuts, glazing, crushed spots, and wear at the splice, and replace it when in doubt. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Will this lanyard work with my adjuster?
faq.a: Check the adjuster maker's approved rope diameters and construction. Not every rope grips properly in every device.

faq.q: Can I cut through a rope lanyard by accident?
faq.a: Yes, a saw will cut any rope lanyard. When cutting near your lanyard, use a steel-core flipline or a second tie-in.

name: Samson True Blue Climbing Rope
title: Samson True Blue 12-Strand Climbing Rope
meta: Samson True Blue is a classic 1/2 in 12-strand climbing rope that arborists have tied in on for years. See how it handles, hitch tips, and the typical price.
tagline: Samson's classic 12-strand arborist climbing line in 1/2 in.
summary: Samson True Blue is a classic 12-strand climbing rope that many arborists learned to climb on. It has a firm hand, a predictable feel with friction hitches, and the easy-to-splice construction of a 12-strand braid.
highlights: 12-strand braid construction
1/2 in (about 12.7 mm) diameter
Works with friction hitches and many devices
Bright color stands out in the canopy
Sold in common arborist lengths

p: True Blue has been a standard on climbing crews for a long time, and its appeal is consistency. A 12-strand braid has no separate cover, so there is no cover slippage, and it is simple to splice an eye for a hardware termination.

On a doubled-rope (MRS) system it works well with traditional friction hitches and a micro pulley to tend slack. Because it is a 12-strand, it can wear differently than a 24-strand line under a mechanical device, so check the device maker's approved rope list before using it on SRS.

Because it has been around so long, True Blue is a useful reference rope. Plenty of trainers and crews know how common hitches behave on it, which makes it a sensible choice for climbers still settling on a system.

body.h: Choosing length and caring for it
p: Pick a length that covers twice the height of your typical tie-in for MRS, or the full height plus tail for SRS. Compare similar lines in climbing rope.

Keep the rope in a bag, away from fuel, bar oil, and sunlight, and run it through your hands before each climb looking for cuts, glazing, and flat or stiff spots. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every use, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is Samson True Blue good for beginners?
faq.a: Many climbers learn on it because it holds friction hitches predictably and is easy to inspect. Training from a qualified climber is still essential.

faq.q: Can I splice True Blue?
faq.a: Yes. 12-strand rope is spliceable, but life-support splices should be done by a trained splicer following Samson's instructions.
